issues.description: The problem statement explicitly asks to "Initialize the ArrayList in a constructor with no arguments" for Farm (i.e., a public no-argument Farm() constructor). The solution implementation, however, only provides a constructor with an int parameter (public Farm(int initialCapacity)) and does not provide a no-argument constructor. Meanwhile the template's Main.java (commented example) expects a no-argument constructor by calling new Farm(). This constructor-parameter mismatch can cause confusion and compilation/runtime issues if students (or tests) expect Farm() to exist and will prevent straightforward use of the provided Main or test code that constructs a Farm without arguments.
issues.suggested_fix: Provide a public no-argument constructor in Farm that initializes the animals list (e.g. public Farm() { this.animals = new ArrayList<>(); }). Optionally keep the existing Farm(int initialCapacity) as an overload. Alternatively, update the problem statement and template to require and demonstrate Farm(int initialCapacity) instead of a no-arg constructor—but keeping a no-arg constructor is the least disruptive fix and matches the exercise description and example usage.

issues.description: The problem statement explicitly requires a no-argument Farm constructor that initializes the internal ArrayList ("Initialize the ArrayList in a constructor with no arguments"). The template’s Main also instantiates the farm using new Farm(). However, the solution implementation only provides a constructor Farm(int initialCapacity) and does not provide a no-arg Farm() constructor. This is an API mismatch: students reading the problem/template expect Farm() but the solution uses a different constructor signature (Farm(int)). This discrepancy creates confusion about the intended constructor and how the animal list should be initialized.
